questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] switching payment providers under a live order saga (opusorganize, apprenticeship/curriculum/16). The orchestrated order saga has been in production for a year on provider P1; the business is moving to provider P2 over a three-week window. At the moment of the switch about 1,800 orders are non-terminal: some authorized but not yet captured (P1 authorizations lapse after 7 days), some waiting on a 3-D Secure confirmation, some in an unknown outcome, and refunds for last month's captures keep arriving. The orchestrator polls every 4 s from 3 replicas, and P2 reports payment statuses with a vocabulary of its own. Write your migration plan before you look: which provider each order's later steps and compensations go to and where that is recorded, how in-flight orders are drained or moved, how P2's statuses enter the saga's states, how historical orders get their provider backfilled, how compensations differ between the two providers, and when P1 may be switched off. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] Every order is pinned to the provider that started its payment: the provider is recorded with the first attempt, and every later capture, void or refund is routed by that record rather than by the current default, because a refund has to go to the provider that holds the money.

[w3] In-flight orders are drained, not moved: new orders start on P2 while P1 orders finish on P1, and the old integration stays up until no non-terminal order is pinned to P1; that drain has a deadline and is watched per provider, since an order nobody drives will sit there indefinitely.
keyPoints.quote: A saga that can hang forever will.

keyPoints.text: [w3] P2's status vocabulary gets its own mapping into the saga's states as a new contract version, kept beside P1's until the drain ends, and a P2 status that lands in no handled state blocks the cutover instead of being discovered later.
[w2] The routing choice is written in the same local transaction as the 'authorizing' state and the attempt row, so a crash mid-switch cannot leave an order whose provider nobody knows.
keyPoints.quote: Persist saga state *with* the step's effect

keyPoints.text: [w2] Historical orders get the provider column backfilled from what each one already recorded (its provider payment id and attempt rows), idempotently and before the router reads the column, so refunds of last month's captures still reach P1.
keyPoints.quote: writes the provider id, the new states and the attempt row in one `tx.Run`

keyPoints.text: [w2] Compensations are chosen per provider and per state (voiding an open authorization differs from refunding a capture, and each provider has its own windows and partial-refund rules), and each stays safe to repeat with that provider's own idempotency key.
keyPoints.quote: Every step and every compensation is idempotent

keyPoints.text: [w2] Unknown outcomes on P1 keep their durable backoff during the drain, but the backoff cap and the attempt limit are checked against P1's switch-off date so no order is still waiting to ask P1 when its credentials go.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — two weeks into the provider switch: a router change sends every capture and refund to P2, including those for orders P1 authorized; P1's API keys are revoked on day 10 while 40 orders still sit in an unknown outcome; a backfill script sets provider = P2 on every row that had no provider value; a new per-provider rate-limit lock is taken on the same database connection as the order lease; re-authorizing old orders on P2 is done as 'void on P1' and then 'authorize on P2' in separate transactions; and old and new worker builds run side by side for half an hour of the rollout. What breaks, how does it show, and what in your plan already prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] Captures and refunds sent to the provider that never held the payment fail or come back unknown; customers who cancelled are not refunded and P1 authorizations lapse uncaptured, because undoing a step means acting on the provider that took the money, not reversing a row.
keyPoints.quote: Compensation is a business action, not a rollback.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Revoking P1 while orders are in an unknown outcome leaves them unable ever to learn whether money moved: they back off until their attempts run out and then show as stuck with the question unanswered, so the switch-off must wait until no P1 order is non-terminal, unknowns included.

[w3] A backfill that defaults a missing provider to the new one silently misroutes every later refund or void of a historical order; the provider has to be derived from the evidence each order recorded before its first provider call, and the per-provider counts checked after the backfill.

[w2] The lease release unlocks everything the session holds, so adding a second advisory lock on the same connection means releasing one order's lease also drops the rate-limit lock (or the reverse), and two workers end up driving what was meant to be exclusive.
keyPoints.quote: It's harmless only while each connection holds exactly one lease.

keyPoints.text: [w2] 'Void on P1' and 'authorize on P2' as two commits is a new crash window: a process death between them leaves an order with no live authorization anywhere and nothing in the scan to resume it, so the migration's new sequences need the same two-commit audit as the original flow.

[w2] The per-order lease guarantees one runner, not a runner that understands the order: an old-build worker can take the lease on a P2 order and mishandle its states, so the code that reads both providers ships everywhere first and routing flips only after every replica runs it.
keyPoints.quote: which is a Postgres session advisory lock

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your provider-migration choices against the alternatives: draining in-flight orders on P1 vs moving them to P2, a gradual percentage rollout vs a one-night cutover, keeping one orchestrator with a provider adapter vs letting each provider's webhooks drive order state, keeping downstream events provider-neutral vs exposing the provider to consumers, and handing the drain's last unresolved orders to people vs compensating them automatically. For each, say what you bought, what it cost, and which requirement put you on that side.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Draining keeps every compensation on the provider that holds the money, at the price of running and paying for two integrations until the last P1 order is terminal; moving orders ends the window sooner but each move is its own void-and-re-authorize saga whose customer-visible effects (a second bank challenge, a declined re-authorization) cannot be taken back.
keyPoints.quote: some steps (sending an email) can't be undone

keyPoints.text: [w3] A percentage rollout limits how many orders an unmapped P2 status can strand and gives time to find one, at the cost of a longer window with two status vocabularies live; a one-night cutover is simpler to reason about but bets every new order on the mapping being complete.
keyPoints.quote: A renamed enum value can silently route an order into a state nothing handles.

keyPoints.text: [w2] One orchestrator with a provider adapter keeps a single place that decides each step and its compensation for every order, whichever provider it uses; letting provider webhooks drive state directly would spread the flow across two integrations' callbacks, at the saving of one polling component.
keyPoints.quote: a coordinator runs steps and, on failure, runs **compensations** in reverse

keyPoints.text: [w2] Downstream consumers keep receiving the same order events whichever provider was used, so shipping and email need no change for the migration; the cost is that the provider detail lives only in the saga's own rows, where support has to look for it.
keyPoints.quote: adds an `OrderEvent` *and* an `OutboxEvent` to the same `DbContext`

keyPoints.text: [w2] The drain's last few orders that P1 cannot resolve before the deadline go to people with their recorded attempts rather than being refunded or voided blind; it costs operator time and buys no double charge and no free order from guessing.
